claims.text: The baseline is an elemental Cr coating deposited directly on zirconium-alloy fuel cladding.
An ultrathin, continuous Al2O3 layer can be deposited between the zirconium alloy and Cr coating by ALD.
The Al2O3 interlayer will prevent premature coating failure by inhibiting elevated-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The Al2O3-modified coating will preserve protection during normal subcritical-water operation.
The Al2O3-modified coating will preserve protection during accident-relevant high-temperature steam exposure.
Protective Cr coatings are an established accident-tolerant-fuel strategy for zirconium-alloy cladding.
Cr coatings can peel and crack during high-temperature steam oxidation.
Premature failure of the unmodified Cr coating is caused by Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
The Al2O3 interlayer acts as a physical and chemical barrier at the Cr–Zr interface.
Dense, stable Al2O3 blocks migration paths for Cr and Zr atoms at elevated temperature.
Blocking Cr and Zr migration prevents detrimental intermetallic phases or an interdiffusion zone that would otherwise degrade the coating.
Al2O3 is chemically inert and retains its integrity in both subcritical water and high-temperature steam.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the Al2O3-modified coating will have a significantly thinner interdiffusion zone after high-temperature steam exposure.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the Al2O3-modified coating will retain better microstructural integrity after high-temperature steam exposure.
Approximately 300°C subcritical PWR water over extended durations is the proposed normal-operation boundary.
Steam exposure up to approximately 1200°C for tens of minutes to one hour is the proposed accident boundary.
The long-term stability of an ultrathin Al2O3 layer under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses is not quantified and may depend on thickness uniformity and adhesion.
Barrier-modified and unmodified controls will be compared after 1200°C steam exposure for 30 minutes and approximately 300°C subcritical-water exposure for 1000 hours.
Interdiffusion-zone thickness and composition, interfacial phases, adhesion, mechanical integrity, and corrosion performance will be measured.

The hypothesis is falsified if the barrier produces no statistically significant reduction in Cr–Zr interdiffusion or interfacial phase formation and its corrosion or mechanical performance is equivalent or worse under both regimes.
